In the foreword of this book, Olive Stevenson addresses the issue of how role affects the interactions of professionals: ‘I have always regretted the intellectual intolerance of each to the other. … I am more than ever convinced that we must take heed of the hidden forces which pull us apart, or inappropriately together, when confronted with behaviour which disturbs us at deep levels’.

[[RunningHead]]

Not Waving But Drowning

Liz Standish

Liz Standish

Liz Standish  

Introduction

This paper describes the first two years' treatment of a young man in his midtwenties whom I shall call John. He was referred within days of my mentioning to a GP that I was looking for a training patient, the speed of the referral reflecting the level of desperation both in patient and referrer.

John's complaint on assessment was that he felt really ill most of the time. When pressed for more detail, all he could describe was ‘this terrible tension’. He often feared he was about to die. Although his history gave rise to grave reservations about his suitability as a training patient, he managed to convince me that I had no choice but to take him on, that he was indeed ‘not waving but drowning’ (Stevie Smith) - the first of many strong counter-transference responses I was to have to this patient.

History

One of the most significant aspects of John's story took place on the day he was due to be born, when his two-year-old sister died in his mother's arms and his mother ‘went funny’ (John's words). John was born some three weeks later. It was a difficult birth and he was born with the cord around his neck. He believes that his father never forgave him for not being a girl to replace the one who died (there were four older brothers), and that this accounted for his sadistic violence being particularly directed towards John. A seventh child, a girl, was born two years after John. This was a working-class family with drink and violence featuring large. It is a bleak picture and not surprising that he also wet the bed until his midteens.

In his late teens he formed a relationship with a girl, which resulted in a pregnancy. They lived together for a few years, and it was the impending birth of his son, combined with a trip to Holland to find work (he is a builder), which gave rise to an acute anxiety attack, the start of his ‘illness’. Attempts to escape from this included binge-drinking, tranquilliser abuse (both largely under control by the time he started treatment) and violence when drunk. His partner left, together with their son, when the latter was aged three. At the time he came to see me, he was living again with his mother and was terrified to leave the house. For years he had pestered the local GP surgery two or three times a week, often out of hours, demanding treatment.

Hermine Hug-Hellmuth (1871-1924) contributed a stream of papers from 1912 onwards on child observation and child analysis, using material from her nephew, Rolf. Her papers ceased in 1924 when Rolf murdered her.

Rolf was the illegitimate son of Hermine's illegitimate sister. After his mother died when he was aged nine, he became more or less uncontrollably delinquent. Though he had guardians, first Viktor Tausk and then Isidor Sadger (Hermine's own analyst), he looked to his aunt for money and affection. The first he got, unwillingly, from her; the second she was probably unable to give. He had his home with this cold, reserved and friendless aunt until 1922 when Sadger put him in a home for delinquent adolescents. A few days before her death she made a will leaving him everything; possibly it was made under his threats.

Kevin Power

Kevin Power

London

Kevin Power  

Bion wrote only one book concerning groups and what happens in them, Experiences in Groups, first published in 1961. It has had great influence on how groups as groups are understood by group practitioners, whether as psychotherapy or as conference tools. This collection, first published in 1985, is a recognition of this influence. It contains seventeen essays by a large variety of contributors, ranging in interest from his First World War experience, work with the War Office and at Northfield Hospital in the Second World War and his work with the Tavistock Clinic in the later 1940s to developments in Basic Assumption theory in the 1980s.

I greatly enjoyed the earlier essays by Trist, Sutherland and de Mare dealing with Bion's pioneering work in the Second World War with the War Office Selection Boards for officers, and his development of the Leaderless Groups for trainees. He challenged the class-basis of officer selection in the work as well as helping to introduce in the most democratic war that the UK had been engaged in, a degree of democracy concerning who should be put forward for training to commission status. In this, the rank and file members of a Scottish regiment were asked to nominate worthy persons from the ranks whom they thought would make good officer material; while the suitability of applicants for officer training remained roughly constant at about 60%, the number of applicants rose by 1500%. This resulted from Bion's doing and must have played an important part in the efficiency of the Army as it grew to be three million strong. However, while the generals were pleased with what he did, his fellow military psychiatrists were not and there seems to have been a professional conspiracy to check his rise to a position where he may have been overseeing all officer selection for the Army. That he continued working hard with the army shows his professionalism as both officer and analyst.

Yet the initial Northfield experiment was halted; the man who only shortly before had played a leading innovative and successful part in the reordering of the vital area of officer selection, took over a wing of this Army Psychiatric Hospital which rapidly became, in embryo, a therapeutic community. This ended six weeks later following a morning visit from War Office personnel after a night of carousing and sexual revelling by the patients in the hospital cinema, probably the result of a tip-off by hospital administration staff (see de Mare's personal memoir in this collection). I wonder whether this debacle of an outcome was Bion (and Rickman) remonstrating, in part, with establishment forces (via the radical treatment programme) for having been thwarted in the officer selection work which had been successful elsewhere, i.e. a demonstration of pique? It is ironic that Foulkes, put in charge of Northfield following Bion's posting elsewhere, had been part of the army which Bion had been fighting against in the Great War. While Bion had then been in the aggressive role of Tank Commander, Foulkes had been working steadily in Telephones and Telegraphs. Bion's aggressivity towards superiors is commented on in several essays, in contrast to Foulkes' gradualist approach (de Mare).

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 73, Part 2, 1992

Does Psychoanalysis Heal?

Robert Caper

Beginning with Freud's controversial admonition to psychoanalysts to model themselves on the surgeon who ‘dresses the wound, but does not heal it’, the author attempts to explore the limits of the therapeutic effect of psychoanalysis. After briefly reviewing the role of projective identification in the transference, and the origin of the analyst's need to be a healer in his anxieties about the strength of his own destructive impulses, he describes certain emotional difficulties that arise in the analyst when he accepts the fact that he can only do analysis. He goes on to suggest that, while psychoanalysis is able to reduce the psychic distance between parts of the patient's mind that have been separated by splitting, this in itself does not provide the patient with a corrective emotional experience, mitigate the severity of his superego, or guide him along the correct developmental path. He further suggests that the analyst's acknowledgement of this limitation - which is equivalent to acknowledging that he can help the patient to grow, but he cannot ‘grow’ him - is part of a state of mind that the analyst must have to do analysis, and that this state of mind helps to distinguish the practice of psychoanalysis from that of other psychotherapies.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 73, Part 2, 1992

Countertransference: The Analyst's Retreat from the Patient's Vantage Point

Evelyne Albrecht Schwaber

As analysts, we may agree with certain basic tenets: we should not impose our truths, whether or not theory-laden; we should maintain the focus on the patient's inner reality, not on how he or she lives in the world - out there; we should be prepared to be surprised, to learn something that hadn't occurred to us; we should look for multiple cues in the clinical data, pay attention to affect and state as may be expressed within the moment, and listen for subtleties that may convey something about how we are being experienced in the transference.

Commentary by a Humanistic and Integrative Psychotherapist

Peter Hawkins

Peter Hawkins

Peter Hawkins  

This case study is both intriguing and elusive. There is so much we as readers do not know and are not told. What is the gender of the psychotherapist? Did she/he tape the session? Did she/he transcribe this session from the tape and if so, how and what was edited? (In its present form I can not see how it could be fifty minutes worth.) What is the nature of the childhood homosexuality with the neighbour and his own ‘cottaging’ with children? Why was there a move to the couch after eighty sessions and what does the therapist think is the link between that and the re-emergence of ‘cottaging’? The therapist writes of being exhausted and feeling inadequate ‘in being “unable” to gain access to what is supposed to be withheld’, we are not told who supposes this withholding - the therapist, the patient or unnamed authorities or theorists. Perhaps this absence of vital information in the presented case is a parallel process to what has been happening in the therapy, where much has been withheld and there have been many secrets.

Like the therapist we must stay aware of how much we do not know, while focusing on what we do know or can surmise by careful attention to the script.

The therapist has clearly established a good therapeutic relationship with the patient, in which difficult and painful material has been able to be gradually shared and explored. The patient in this session has not only been able to get in touch with his rage and hatred, but has also been able to mention the here and now anger towards the therapist.

If I were the supervisor of this therapist I would focus on what I see as the key turning point of this session which remains as an ‘unfinished gestalt’. The patient J brings himself to the point of confronting the therapist with his anger:

… and you were not here on Mnday (note: I was away by prearrangement) … suddenly feel very angry about that. Monday it felt OK … didn't register, suppressed… you're the focus, target … for about 30 years of rage, that's the picture forming.

Beyond Countertransference: The Therapist's Subjectivity in the Therapeutic Process by Joseph Natterson. Published by Jason Aronson Inc., 1991; 242 pages.

David Mann

David Mann

London

David Mann  

This is a bold book. Natterson's thesis is that the therapist's subjective life is co-equal to that of the client in creating the therapeutic transaction. The book's title, Beyond Countertransference, reflects the author's view that traditional notions of countertransference are too limiting to encompass what he is trying to describe. The idea of countertransference has developed considerably in the last hundred years of psychoanalysis. Natterson points out, rightly in my view, that, even though most therapists would recognise that their countertransference means more than just a neurotic disturbance in the therapist, the term still carries some of its historical and implicit baggage, namely that, even in its widest definition, countertransference still implies a disturbance in the therapist/analyst and merely describes the therapist as one who responds to the client.

Natterson argues that because Freud believed that instinctual drives motivated our psychological lives, a belief that led to an intrapsychic theory of personality development, this caused him to under-value the significance of interpersonal factors. Natterson recommends two important changes of emphasis in psychoanalytic work; first, that there needs to be less emphasis on drives in favour of intersubjective, interpersonal factors; and second, that countertransference, which derives from an intrapsychic orientation, needs to be subordinated to concepts of intersubjectivity. Natterson's suggestion is to acknowledge the therapist's subjective contribution to the therapeutic process as potentially useful and proactive as well as reactive. He suggests that psychotherapists think in terms of an intersubjective process between client and therapist and confine the term countertransference to its original meaning of a neurotic disturbance in the analyst in response to the client's material.

The author cites a number of other writers who have paved the way for this approach: Ferenczi's ‘mutual analysis’, Alexander's ‘corrective emotional experience’, Winnicott's ‘holding environment’ and Gedo's ‘non-interpretative intervention’. He writes: ‘All human two-person transactions share fundamental meaning: each party attempts to influence the other with his or her view of the universe to persuade the other of the rightness of his or her view’ (p. 28).

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Like mathematics, or science, psycho-analytic psychotherapy can be pure or applied. But, can we ask: how pure is pure? And when is it so impure that it isn't it at all?

There is no doubt that Ruth Barnett's reflections on psychotherapy twice or threetimes a week strike a cord. Frequency is important, but what importance and how important? These questions affect psychotherapists. A good deal of status for the therapist may often attach to how near to the psycho-analytic five-times-a-week he works. Nevertheless, as Ruth Barnett says, the frequency of sessions significantly affects patients - though perhaps in different ways. There is often a need to tailor the frequency to the patient. More equals more intense, equals better, does not necessarily apply. The theme is taken up by Anthony Ryle and his colleagues who have been venturing into a new, and integrative, world by alloying cognitive therapy with some central aspects of psycho-analytic theory and practice - to form a ‘cognitive-analytic therapy’ (in contrast to cognitive behavioural therapy). They claim that such a blend allows a shortening of the duration of therapy, and argue strongly for the need for such time-limited methods in the hard-pressed public services.

Linda Hoag also writes about an unconventional adaptation of psychotherapy - to therapeutic work in a general practice. Counselling and psychotherapy in general practices is rapidly becoming less unconventional; more and more therapists and counsellors are being taken on by doctors. Necessarily there is a need for increasing attention to this form of activity. Linda Hoag is concerned with the extraneous pressures which intrude on the work in the medical surgery. Because of the high pressure of medical anxieties and work loads, there are special difficulties in creating a place of safety. Linda Hoag describes the work inherent in holding to a standard and consistent frame or setting for the work. There is also an added spin-off from this work in terms of the sense of containment the psychotherapist can contribute to the practice itself.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon  

It could easily have been Sandor Ferenczi's fate to have been an interesting but relatively minor figure in the history of psychoanalysis. It was, after all, he who conducted the first training analysis (with Ernest Jones), who introduced Melanie Klein to her analyst Karl Abraham, who proposed the creation of the International Psychoanalytical Association, and who was the first Professor of Psychoanalysis (at the University of Budapest under the short-lived revolutionary government of Bela Kim in 1919).

Ferenczi's reputation was not helped, to put it mildly, by rumours (said to have originated with his former analysand Jones) that he had sexual relations with patients and by Jones' claim in his biography of Freud that he - Ferenczi - had become psychotic, thus discrediting much of his later work. Ferenczi's fate as someone who might well be ‘interesting’ but whose work was not really worth serious consideration seemed to be sealed when he was prayed in aid, albeit critically, by the psychoanalytic renegade Jeffrey Masson. In his book attacking Freud on the issue of sexual abuse of children, The Assault on Truth, Masson republished Ferenczi's paper 'Confusion of tongues between adults and the child', claiming Ferenczi as one who had rediscovered what Freud had suppressed. Even those seemingly better disposed towards Ferenczi have contributed to his minimal reputation, recognising his ‘influence’ but only as something that had been superseded by later generations, particularly those of Klein and Balint and their followers.

British Journal of Medical Psychology, Volume 64, Part 3, 1991

The Maintenance of Psychotherapy Skill Aquisition: A Two-Year Follow-up

Steve Moss, Frank Margison and Ken Godbert

A two-year follow-up study investigated changes in interview behaviour of 11 therapists who had previously been trained in the conversational model of psychotherapy by a combined videotaped microteaching and supervision package. Results generally showed the acquired skills had been well maintained. However, there was a large increase in the giving of information and explanation, a behaviour explicitly discouraged within the conversational model. In addition, the response to verbal cues, a positive model behaviour, decreased over the follow-up period.



Journal of Analytical Psychology, Volume 36, Number 4, 1991

Immersions in Ambiguity: The Labyrinth and the Analytic Process

Caroline Savitz

In this paper I have used the Cretan myth of the labyrinth, with its devouring minotaur at the centre, as archetype and metaphor for describing the internal world of the schizoid personality. The schizoid person creates impenetrable and inextricable labyrinthine walls as protection from interpersonal violation and from the internal minotaur of intolerable suffering, memory, and anxiety. The imprisoned minotaur, split-off and disavowed, begins to govern the personality, and the terrified ego flees to the periphery of the personality. I have examined the transference implications of this difficult labyrinthine structure through the use of clinical illustrations, and have discussed the capacity of the labyrinth to open up to the lost underworld of suffering. False resolutions and escapes from the labyrinth through flights into meaning, including Jung's relationship to the mandala and the labyrinth, are also considered.

The ‘Prehistory’ of the Idea of Transference Nathan M. Kravis

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

In January 1893 Breuer and Freud published a preliminary communication. It ushered in the twentieth century view of human nature. It is now one hundred years on. We asked a number of psycho-analysts and psychotherapists for a contemporary reaction to those origins in the 1890's. Mostly there was an enthusiastic response to reflecting on our past and where we have come. These papers form a substantial section in this issue of the Journal.

David Smith pinpoints the moment in Freud's work on the preliminary communication and the Studies on Hysteria when the notion of the ‘unconscious’ emerges with a new and more precise meaning as the cornerstone of psycho-analytic theory.

Sabbadini reviews the case of Katharina whose identity has recently been unearthed by Peter Swales; and thus some estimate of her ‘follow-up’ condition after her consultation with Freud can now be made. David Bell looks at the original cases too. But he views them in the light of modern psychiatric and psycho-analytic practice. The clinical absence of similar symptoms in patients today may, he concludes, merely represent a difference in presenting symptoms. The narcissistic and borderline patients so commonly reported in contemporary psycho-analysis are the direct descendents of nineteenth century hysterics. They have the same core psychopathology. Such patients clearly have a very variable method of presenting themselves which is highly culturally dependent; perhaps dependent on the changing culture of the ‘clinic’ itself. This may go some way to explain why such patients seem so much harder to treat today than one hundred years ago.

James Grotstein plots the development of psycho-analysis since its inception as a retreat from the originating idea of the unconscious, and the need to rediscover the forgotten path. It is the ubiquitous sense of the ‘alter ego’, overgrown by the unifying, scientific conception of the structural theory of ego-id-superego. Like Grotstein, Salomon Resnik revises the view of hysteria as an internal theatrical drama played out with real though unwitting accomplices in a stagey manner. And like Bell he relates these to the currently prominent narcissistic personalities.

The Psychotherapy Register

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny  

I have been asked to explain the structural changes that are taking place in UKSCP and to describe how these will lead to the formation of a register of psychotherapists early in 1993. I shall briefly survey the present balanced structure, describe the most recent changes and show how they will work in practice.

After the collapse of the profession's joint working party, the Rugby psychotherapy conference was started, which went on to become the UKSCP in January of 1989. This was achieved by much work and was based on the concept of having semi-autonomous sections which would contain the different varieties of psychotherapy. Sections make their own rules in their own way, provided that the rules and criteria make sense to the other sections and fit within the agreed baseline of training criteria. These are: graduate level entry, MA equivalent content, supervised treatment of clients and training in the appropriate management of the trainee's own involvement in the therapy process. This will mean therapy or analysis for some kinds of psychotherapy and other forms of training for other kinds of psychotherapy. In either case it is a requirement that the training shows that the arrangements are appropriate to the task of their own particular kind of therapy.

For some time there has been a significant shift towards a more uniform standard of training by a subtle kind of upgrading that has gone on almost unnoticed. In order to stay in line within their own Section, member organisations have been raising their training requirements. Two examples: one organisation in the Analytic Psychotherapy Section used to recommend that its trainees have own therapy; now they demand it. One of the Jung trainings used to require twice weekly analysis; now it requires thrice. We have kept a steady pressure on the Sections to produce criteria that are distinctive and satisfactory.

The Council of UKSCP is made up of one delegate from each of the eight Sections and one each from British Psychological Society, the Royal College of Psychiatrists, the Association of University Teachers of Psychiatry and The Tavistock Clinic. In addition there are five officers and four ordinary members who are elected at the AGM from among the delegates to Conference. All committees are created by Council and report to Council.

Countertransference and Older Clients edited by Bonnie Genevay and Renee S Katz. Published by Sage Publications Ltd, London, 1990; 192 pages; £25.00 hardback, £12. 75 paperback.

Ruth Porter

Ruth Porter

London

Ruth Porter  

Professor Robert Kastenbaum, in his excellent foreword to this book, describes the terror we feel when confronted by old age and its eventual accompaniments: physical decrepitude, mental deterioration, helplessness and death. He notes, and the book describes, the evasions and defences we use to avoid panic when faced with these issues in our patients, our kith and kin and ourselves. Kastenbaum quotes the twentieth century North American poet Winfield Townley Scott: ‘Whom do the mourners see? Themselves. Themselves. …’. This is what the book is about: the professional helpers, and our own, feelings when we are in touch with elderly individuals.

Countertransference is defined in its widest sense as all the feelings that are experienced by those who work with the elderly. The book discusses how helpers can become aware of, acknowledge, understand and use these feelings to help their clients. The most common countertransference reactions are named as ‘anger and resentment; inadequacy and failure; powerlessness and lack of control; frustration and guilt; sadness and grief; fears or aging, emotional pain, losses, dependency and death’.

The contributors are psychoanalytically-experienced psychotherapists with a background of sociology and social work. So this is a practical book. It contains a number of guidelines and check-lists, and a self-awareness quiz to test our own feelings and fears of decrepitude and death. Two tables in the final chapter set out the effect of the professional helpers' countertransference responses on the client; and early signs of negative countertransference. The authors make the point that these responses in the helpers come not only from their reactions to their clients but also from their upbringing and development, their prejudices, and their past and present relationships with family, friends and colleagues. The focus is on the professional helpers and on case work rather than on psychodynamic concepts of transference and countertransference in the elderly as described in the 1970s and 1980s by, for example, Pearl King, Peter Hilderbrand and George Pollock.

The Psychotherapy Register

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny  

At a meeting of the United Kingdom Standing Conference for Psychotherapy on Saturday 7 March 1992 a series of working papers describing the organisation of a register of psychotherapists was discussed, amended and accepted.

What has been agreed is to have a Registration Board which is made up of appointees from the Special and Institutional Member Organisations, plus representatives from those Sections which can meet the training standards. Only delegates of accredited training organisations may sit on the Board. There is provision for an extra seat for the British Psycho-Analytical Society. The structure is such that the Board cannot have its decisions changed by any of the bodies of UKSCP. It is insulated from the Council and therefore from the AGM. Even the Appeals Committee can only refer cases back to it for reconsideration.

The Training Standards Committee will comprise delegates appointed by the Registration Board and the Council. The Sections will continue to have a pivotal role in the regular scrutiny of Member Organisations and in setting specific standards for their own kind of therapy.

Registration will be at two levels: basic and advanced. An outline of the level of basic training has been agreed. The essentials are that entry to training will be at graduate level or equivalent, and a ground year must be completed before training. This caters for trainees who do not come from any associated professional background. The curriculum content will be roughly equivalent to a part-time MA. The question of training therapy is dealt with by each Section devising its own model appropriate to itself.

Disciplinary matters will continue to be dealt with in each Member Organisation and, if that is not satisfactory, in the Sections. We hope that recourse to Council for complaints and malpractice will be extremely rare. Of course when we get to a statutory Register we will have to devise a disciplinary committee.

There is now the basis of a structure that will become the process that can lead to a statutory register in due course. It has always been the intention of UKSCP to move to a register that is regulated by statute, which was signalled when we resolved to seek to become a Competent Authority for psychotherapy.

International Review of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 18, Part 4, 1991

The Freud-Ferenczi Controversy - A Living Legacy

Axel Hoffer

The painful personal and professional controversy which arose between Sigmund Freud and his favourite pupil, Sandor Ferenczi, towards the end of the latter's life, is examined first from an historical perspective and then as a metaphor for conflicts universally experienced by the analyst in daily work. Their disagreement originates in Ferenczi's challenge - articulated in his techniques of ‘relaxation’ and ‘indulgence’ - to Freud's principle of ‘abstinence’. By 1930, their views on the analytic relationship had become so highly polarized that Freud came to represent the emphasis on thinking and frustration while Ferenczi stood for gratification and feeling. Ultimately, their controversy centred around Freud's emphasis on the work of remembering and reconstructing in contrast to Ferenczi's emphasis on re-living and re-experiencing. The relevance of these controversies to current views on what aspects of the repetition in psycho-analysis are therapeutic is illustrated by a clinical example from the literature of a patient who wants to hold the analyst's hand during the reexperiencing of an early traumatic event. The continuing influence of their controversy on contemporary debates about the nature of the analytic relationship and the analyst's participation in the repetition compulsion through re-enactments is highlighted.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 72, Part 4, 1991

Encapsulation as a Defence against the Fear of Annihilation

Earl Hopper

Encapsulation is defined as a defence against annihilation anxiety. A theoretical orientation concerning the origins of this kind of anxiety is outlined, and the causal efficacy of early traumata is emphasized. On this basis, encapsulation is conceptualized as an introjective process through which attempts are made to fuse and confuse parts of the self with parts of the lost and abandoning object. Clinical and case history data from several patients are presented. A number of topics for further research are suggested. The literature is reviewed, and the current use of ‘encapsulation’ is linked to earlier work on disavowal, foreclosure and resourceless dependence.

Dorothy Daniell

Dorothy Daniell

Dorothy Daniell  

This book is both a general study of the HIV/AIDS virus and its implications,- and an account of the planning, carrying out and following through of a one day experimental workshop on ‘Group responses to the Aids Crisis’.

Angela Molnos, well-known as a group analyst and innovator in the field of shortterm psychotherapy, writes in her introduction: ‘This book addresses a wide range of professionals as well as the general reader who is keen to reflect upon the ways in which our shared unconscious seems to react to the spread of the HIV infection, which is just one of the life threatening phenomena of our age’. The key word in this passage is unconscious. The shared unconscious attitudes of the general public and more particularly of professionals, carers and those directly related to HIV/AIDS patients, were brought into greater conscious awareness through the focused experience of a group of sixty people, gathered in a one-day experimental workshop in December 1987.

Part I of the book describes the retrovirus HIV in terms of its physical effects, but also most illuminatingly in terms of its psychological effect in undermining and reversing many of our social values and expectations. Most profoundly, sex from being associated with love and pleasure becomes associated with fatal disease; blood, the necessity for life, becomes the carrier of death. Angela Molnos writes about the destructive impact of this reversal upon our sense of ‘meanings’ with a kind of passionate sadness. She goes on to describe the relevance of group analysis in providing a means of sharing experience and so increasing our available energy and understanding to meet the crisis.

Part II of the book is a detailed description of the workshop ‘from the first idea to the final format’. It will be of the greatest interest to all those involved in group analytic work as it gives an extremely clear and honest description of the day from the point of view of convenors, staff and participants. As would be expected, particular attention is given to areas of difficulty and dissension. The day began with four short talks by eminent speakers who are pioneering in the work. There followed small groups, a ‘Non-Fish bowl’ experience, further small groups and a plenary discussion.

Commentary by an Independent Group Psycho-Analyst

Ken Wright

Ken Wright

Ken Wright  

Introduction

I shall have very little to say about how I would have conducted this session if I had been the therapist. Any particular session is a joint creation of the therapeutic couple. This particular session is the product of a joint working and shared understanding developed over two and a halt years - as ‘outsiders’ to the therapy, we are excluded from that shared perspective as much as we are from the intimate events of someone else's marriage. What we can do in an exercise like this, without being too presumptuous, is to expose the process of our own thinking and to share with others the working concepts which we use in therapy.

Background Information

I will start with the background data in order to show how the various details of the ‘text’ mobilise thoughts and impressions in the therapist's mind, how these begin to come together and make a ‘story’ about the patient, and how when this occurs we feel we are beginning to understand the patient. I shall italicise fragments of the therapist's ‘text’. My own associations will follow in normal typescript.

The Patient

Man of 40 … member of religious community … practising homosexual since childhood.

Thoughts about monks … retreating from life … searching for something … trying to find or serve God … God the Father perhaps.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Experimental psychology started as a scientific discipline in its own right at a point roughly contemporary with the emergence of psycho-analysis. Not much interchange has happened between them over the lifetime of the two disciplines, and it has tended to get less as time goes on. However, remarkable experimental studies in the development of the very young infant have accumulated and recently there has been an increasing psycho-analytic interest. Perhaps the most important work summarising and creating a framework for this experimental work is the book by Daniel Stern. He has in fact brought together experimental psychology of the neonate with psycho-analytic theories, and come to conclusions which conflict with those of Margaret Mahler, but perhaps substantiate certain object-relations ideas.

Maxine Anderson, in this issue of the Journal, has written a balanced critique of Stern's work. With her American background she shows how there is a distinct tendency for Stern to remain confined within the American ego-psychology school. Despite this, Stern's work is of immense value in putting to test the durability of psycho-analytic theories of development.

John Hill's recollections of his supervisor, Wilfred Bion, are personal; and therefore valuable to the increasingly large number of psychotherapists who did not have personal acquaintance with Bion. As one of those who did not, I find it remarkable that Bion's sayings seem as vivid to those who heard him as his writings do to his readers. And as time goes on there seems to be an unending supply of new anecdotes about him and what he has pronounced upon. Often what he has said has been profoundly and humorously critical of psycho-analysis, but he is adhered to no less for that.

Another gnomic figure who haunts the psycho-analytic and psychotherapeutic worlds in Britain is Ignacio Matte-Blanco. He is an Italian philosopher who trained in psycho-analysis in London just before the Second World War, and has thereafter attempted to conjoin logic with psycho-analytic analysis. His ideas on non Aristotelian logic and the unconscious have gained respect and recent adherents. Is it accessible, though, to people who quiver at the knees when faced with the symbols of mathematical logic sprinkled densely on a page. The answer Ian Mordant gives is emphatically, yes. His article takes us, slowly enough for the most timid, through the basic ideas, gradually accelerating as we become more confident. For those of fainter heart, Gail Yariv contributes to a theme that is familiar to readers of this Journal; what is psychotherapy. Is it art, is it science? Yariv argues that such a dichotomy is itself destructive of useful thinking. It is a dichotomy that smacks of pathological splitting.

Psychotherapy in the General Practice Surgery: Considerations of the Frame

Linda Hoag

Linda Hoag

The Bungalow, 57 The Broadway, Shifnal, Shropshire TE11 8BB

Linda Hoag  

This paper is an attempt to explore how maintenance of a secure frame, or provision of secure-frame moments within the deviant frame of the general practice surgery, may have a positive effect on patients in therapy. This assumption is supported by data from my own practice where attempts to secure the frame in several ways contributed to changes in number of failed appointments, premature termination and number of sessions attended.

While the therapist's maintenance of the basic ground rules in relation to the therapy is shown to create a background of safety, a hold or container, and a defined therapeutic space within which communication between patient and therapist can lead to resolution of conflicts and personal growth, it is also suggested that there can be positive effects on the wider setting of the surgery and its staff.

The psychotherapist or counsellor in general practice is in a pioneering role, and may get caught up in her own ambivalence in terms of needing to be seen as acceptable and useful to the medical hierarchy in which she works and, at the same time, needing to provide for patients the setting necessary for psychotherapeutic work to take place. Flexibility of the therapist in managing this situation must be balanced by a willingness to acknowledge the positive potential contained within the basic ground rules, and an ability to examine carefully the effects of deviations from these ground rules.

It is hoped that the material presented here will stimulate other therapists working in general practice surgeries to examine the frame, work to secure it, and acknowledge the effects on the patient of deviation from it. There is also certainly a need for further research on the effects on the wider setting and its staff of having a therapist working as part of the primary health care team.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

It is pleasant to find objective evidence of the beneficial outcome of psychotherapy. Alasdair Macdonald devised an interesting measurement: the numbers of visits to the general practitioner before and after treatment. This is a useful measurement as it overcomes the bias laid on conscious assessment by the patient which is inherent in ‘consumer satisfaction’ studies. The fall in those visits which he found even after the briefest psychotherapeutic treatment is important clinically, as well as administratively.

The preferred method of assessing outcome which psychotherapists usually adopt is an attempt at gauging change in the internal world of the patient. More or less unmeasurable quantitatively, much of the psychotherapy literature is trying to describe qualitative assessments of the internal world of patients. In Sue Gottlieb's paper she describes the nature of possible internal change in a patient who has suffered a significant early deficit. The object's capacity to function as a transformational object significantly affected the internal world and its state of integration in the face of experiences to be metabolised. Maxine Anderson takes up a very similar theme but looks at it in terms of an essential conflict, rather than an historical deficit. The capacity for the object to perform the same containing (transforming) function is in this case hampered by the attacks upon that object. These two papers taken together pursue opposite trajectories in the deficit-versus-conflict debate; and they bear comparison on this dimension.

The burden of responsibility placed on a defective external object is emphasised by Paul Tibbles and Gillian Russell. They show the way a schizophrenic girl deals with an uncommunicative (uncontaining, or defectively transforming) mother through generating a symbiotic world to live in. It appeared that all three parameters - the daughter's schizophrenia, the mother's uncommunicativeness, and the symbiosis between them - changed together (and each for the better) in the course of a brief treatment.

[[RunningHead]]

An Ambivalent Heritage

Rosemary Jackson

Rosemary Jackson

East Pennard, Somerset BA4 6TW

Rosemary Jackson  

I have always felt a profound ambivalence towards the legacy of analysis and therapy, on both personal and political levels. This has taken me in and out of practice as a psychotherapist and in the summer of 1989, whilst still seeing clients, I found myself writing out some of the contradictions in the form of fiction. It started with a story about a psychodrama workshop - based loosely on a weekend I had attended - its protagonist being a man familiar with psychoanalytic work and theory. He was highly sceptical of the apparently rapid healing on offer through the catharsis of group theatre and his doubts and misgivings run through the resulting tale, ‘Future Perfect’. Like him, the narrative is torn between analytic insight and a less detached position that asks whether his scruples and knowledge are not after all the very things that prevent him from participating fully and so benefiting from the experience.

Other stories quickly followed, exploring parallel and related themes, and a collection of tales about psychotherapy emerged and was published early in 1991 - The Eye of the Buddha and Other Therapeutic Tales (Jackson 1991). There are many dilemmas being worked out through them, but one of the key ones is the tension between what we might term ‘orthodox’ analysis and more radical or ‘new age’ alternatives. The title story, ‘The Eye of the Buddha’, is perhaps the closest to an allegory of the various conflicts I was trying to resolve. There an analyst (male) is married to a Buddhist (female), and although I use to the full the licence of fiction to exaggerate, their rather extreme positions are in fact only magnifications of arguments I have actually heard. On the one hand, the psychoanalyst's dogmatic defence of his profession and what he regards as its monopoly on truth, on the other, the mystic's turning away from what she sees as the bigotries of a depressingly rational science - though her embrace of alternatives may be an even more fanatical and exclusive belief system. Their conflict comes to a dramatic head and puts their marriage dangerously on the rocks, as Ilse attacks her husband's analytic colleagues and assumptions.

Commentary by a Pluralist Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist

Jean White

Jean White

Jean White  

Work with a sexually abused patient is inevitably slow and difficult and I am impressed by the therapist's patience and sensitivity in holding this man's ‘skeletal’ sense of self. Although the patient has well-entrenched schizoid and sexualising defences, his internal world is by no means completely closed off, and he also sounds extremely persistent in struggling to get what what he needs from the therapy. The therapist's approach is clearly supportive and containing, but I wonder if the therapy might feel more containing to the patient if the therapist were to adopt a more venturesome interpretative approach.

It is, of course, so much easier to comment on a session with hindsight than to think under the pressure of the patient's projections and whilst keeping a part of oneself available to experience the transference/countertransference matrix. Firstly, I would like to inform my comments on how I might have managed this session differently with some theoretical speculations about the data which have been helpfully provided about the patient's background, life history and use of the therapy so far. I would want to do this also if I were preparing to sit in the room with the patient - not for the purpose of maintaining a rigid theoretical framework from which to make interpretations, but as a means of holding myself in my therapeutic role and enhancing my capacity to observe and to think in the session. I would therefore be prepared either to let go of my speculations completely or modify them considerably if I were then to experience something very different coming from the patient.

Although the actual sex of the therapist is not mentioned, the patient seems to be expressing a preference for experiencing the therapist as a ‘strong or firm’ father or substitutive penis as opposed to the much more terrifying threat of emotional engulfment by the mother.

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode  

Since this book was first published in 1983, awareness of the reality of child abuse has increased dramatically, together with recognition of the help that professionals can offer its victims. The Tavistock Clinic workshop on which the book was based has continued to flourish, with increasing numbers of workers making referrals, encouraged perhaps by the attempts recorded here to make sense of the kind of experience that normally engenders rage, despair or numbness. It is sometimes difficult, when reading the book, to keep in mind just how much of a pioneering venture it was: that it was widely argued, on theoretical as well as on practical grounds, that severely deprived children in care could not be ‘suitable cases for treatment’.

The case studies collected here make it very understandable that this should have been so. The children concerned had suffered from every conceivable permutation of calamitous circumstances - single parent families, mental illness in the parents, abandonment from birth, multiple changes of children's home or foster parents - though actual abuse was not particularly prominent among these. Often a referral was made when a placement for fostering or adoption had broken down, after previous high hopes. The authors make the point that there may well have been something atypical about this sample of children in that all of them had inspired at least one worker with concern or affection or the feeling that something must be done. This did not stop the experience of their therapists from being one of virtually intolerable painful bombardment: always mental, often physical. Again and again the therapists were made to feel unwanted, useless, insignificant, left out, helpless against the manifestations of evil; or again, the repository of a seemingly two-dimensional child's capacity to feel pain. Three examples remain particularly in the mind. A little girl of four, who had been abruptly removed from her home because of sexual abuse by the father, subjected a doll to various amputations - of a ‘sister’, an arm, a leg- because ‘I like doing it’: finally, with a flourish, producing ‘a bloody mess’ while the therapist sat trying not to cry.

Rob Weatherill

Rob Weatherill

Dublin

Rob Weatherill  

This book carefully examines the fate, stability, coherence and status of ‘the self’ n a world of accelerating change, of ephemerality - the postmodern world of exhilaration and violence.

If human identity is constructed in a social milieu through object relating, then clearly the quality of that environment, the existence or not of essential supportive conditions, will be reflected in the stability of that selfhood. And what most theorists of modernity agree on is that the achievement of some coherent selfhood has become increasingly problematic and, for some theorists, even undesirable. Psychoanalysis, however, is well placed to show how, firstly, social conditions structure internal states and, secondly, to supply criteria by which modern social experience can be evaluated.

Contradiction, fluidity, multiplicity, plurality describe both the terror and the excitement of modernity. Frosh contrasts well modernism and postmodernism. Schaverien's book The Revealing Image is a welcome and innovative study of the role of the image in the therapeutic relationship. The author explores previously uncharted territory in art therapy focusing on the complex transference phenomena involved. She has coined the term ‘Analytical Art Psychotherapy’ to describe her theoretical approach rooted in Jungian analytical psychology and the philosophy of Cassirer. In forming her ideas she draws on many other disciplines - philosophy, religion and art - which makes for rich and interesting reading. The book is generously illustrated with both colour and black and white images, as befits an art therapy text. Although primarily a theoretical study, the author breathes life into her ideas through frequent allusions to clinical material; indeed one entire chapter is a case study.

The early chapters explore the nature of transference and counter-transference in relation to art therapy, and link Jung's ideas of the alchemical metaphor with an understanding of the transforming potential of art therapy. The author then goes on to explore her concept of the ‘scapegoat’ in art therapy in which feelings and thoughts are attributed to, or disposed of, in the picture. She makes use of anthropological findings to support her thesis, making this one of the most exciting and original parts of the book. This linking of apparently unconnected ideas from a variety of cultures lends an added dimension to her ideas.

Analysts and therapists have daily to cope with a difficulty, the fact that many of their patients' most important feelings are felt as infinite. For example that boundless despair so often apparent in a depressive patient is a felt infinity. This infinity often masks other unconscious infinities, such as those of boundless guilt, grandiosity or omniscience. It is thus an important aspect of Matte Blanco's work that it draws attention to the whole subject of infinite outcomes. The examination of such outcomes is aided in this paper by illustrations of some useful ways of picturing infinity.

Matte Blanco's work also contains a suggestion as to a major source of these infinities and, in discussing this, this paper will enable an analyst or therapist to look for this source of a particular patient's pathological infinities.

The paper concludes by suggesting some extensions to Matte Blanco's work and some possible auras for future work.

I read this book wearing two hats and had two different reactions to it: as a group therapist I found it both exciting and frustrating; as a sociologist I found it a disappointment. This certainly involves some splitting on my part but I think it also reflects the comparatively distinct areas of reality with which the two areas are concerned.

As a group therapist, my one experience of a large group run along group-analytic lines was as part of the IGA Introductory course some ten years ago. My memory is that I spent most of the nine or ten sessions in a state of near-frozen panic, measuring the distance between myself and the door and wondering if I could make it before ‘they’ got me. People said it became easier after you said something and during the penultimate session I managed to say something. I felt no better.

It makes an awful lot of sense now to see this as the starting point of a development, which if I could have stayed with it would move through hate (I did not experience that possibility at the time but looking back I can see it was there), and, by means of dialogue, to an ‘impersonal fellowship’, the state of Koinonia which gives the book its title. There is much that is exciting and interesting about this book, from people who have now carried research into large and median group processes for a number of years.

There is also much that is frustrating about it. Other reviewers have commented on the style, and I found the attempts at conceptualisation frustrating and confusing, obscuring rather than clarifying. I got much more from it when I gave up trying to learn the definitions of macroculture, microculture, subculture, bioculture, socioculture, idioculture and understand their use. Even when the definitions are comparatively clear, as in the author's contrast of structure and system, the use is confusing. Whilst the book admirably tries to make bridges to other disciplines such as philosophy and sociology, it does so in a haphazard and over-general way, sometimes employing outdated sources and resorting to shopping lists of names and theories. I found particularly irksome the failure to full reference quotations, and felt sure that in some cases, despite quotation marks, I was being presented with a loose paraphrase of the original.

Already, in 1925, as Claudia Zanardi reminds us in her fascinating introduction, Freud was defending himself vigorously against feminist demands that women be recognised as ‘completely equal in position and worth’. Zanardi's twenty-three Essential Papers on women's psychology bear witness to seven decades of fruitful debate between psychoanalysts and feminists. Lucienne Serrano and Elaine Hoffman Baruch, editors of Women Analyze Women, visited consulting-rooms ranging in style from ‘palazzi to monastic cells’ to interview nineteen famous analysts and writers about the impact of gender on their professional lives. There is much overlap between the concerns of these two sets of editors including their choice of contributors. Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel, Joyce McDougall, Luce Irigiray, Juliet Mitchell, Jessica Benjamin, and feminist academics, Julia Kristeva, Nancy Chodorow and Dorothy Dinnerstein, all chat personally in Women Analyze Women about the theories they expound in their Essential Papers.

Zanardi chooses a wonderfully diverse mix of ‘classic’ analytic and feminist papers that focus around essential questions posed by Freud - on female penis envy, the wish for a child, lesbianism, masochism and super ego development. Yet, ironically, the most notable omission is of Freud's own provocative yet rich papers on female sexuality. He is, it appears, just too male-biased to include. This is fair enough except that the book revolves around disagreements and reinterpretations of his theories. I would have liked to have been able to turn back to what he himself said rather than having to rely on inevitably biased synopses.

It is also very striking that although the Essential Papers ostensibly include writings by British as well as French and US feminists, there is only one British feminist contributor - Juliet Mitchell. And she, we are told in the introduction, has not been particularly influential in the US. The only ‘classic’ British analytic papers are by Klein (1945) and by Winnicott (1966), the latter including case-material about a male patient rather than women. Serrano and Baruch's book Women Analyze Women includes interviews with Dinora Pines, Enid Balint and Hanna Segal as well as Mitchell.

Transactional analysis is a psychotherapy, originally developed in America in the 1950s, with a membership of 8,000 practitioners in 52 countries. Its founder was Eric Berne who trained as a psychoanalyst at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute. Dr Clarkson describes Berne's influences as a background understanding of Freud, Klein and Fairbairn combined with the intrapsychic phenomenological interests of Federn and the social-developmental emphases of Erikson. His writing assumes familiarity with psychoanalytic, ego psychological and object-relations theories.

Dr Clarkson describes Berne's theoretical approach as being:

… an extension to the in-depth emphasis of psychoanalysis with its singular focus on intrapsychic dynamics. Transactional analysis as a theory of psychotherapy, however, integrates intrapsychic dynamics with interpersonal behaviours in an innovative reactive manner within a humanistic/existential framework of values.

Berne, himself, was a prolific writer and used an approachable style and language that made his theories a cult for the 1960s. However, his concepts and theories have often gone unacknowledged as his influence has been absorbed into popular vocabulary and infiltrated other psychotherapies (for example, the concept of the ‘child’ in a person, giving ‘strokes’ to a person, playing a ‘game’ with another person). Furthermore, the theories have been trivialised by others who do not grasp the theoretical depth behind the ‘user friendly’ language.

Since the 1960s, many writers and theorists have added to the body of knowledge.

Roger Horrocks

Roger Horrocks

Roger Horrocks  

Dear Sir

Diana Birkett's paper on ‘Psychoanalysis and War’ (British Journal of Psychotherapy 8(3)) raises some very important issues within psychotherapy, and within an overall psychological understanding of human beings. To a non-analytical therapist, the analytical treatment of war and other social conflicts often seems bizarre. It reminds me of Margaret Thatcher's celebrated dictum: ‘There is no such thing as society!’

To see war simply as the projection of many individual sadisms leaves out the social conflicts underpinning it. And if social conflict itself is seen only as projected intrapsychic conflict, then history itself disappears. Are we to say that the English Civil War, the French Revolution, the American War of Independence and Civil War, the Russian Revolution, are without historical and social significance? This suggests that such social forces as feudalism and capitalism (which I assume came into collision in the above revolutions) are themselves non-existent or, if they do exist, have no psychological consequences for the human being.

It strikes me that there is a blurring between cause and effect here. Based on the unimpeachable observation that war allows the expression of infantile conflicts and primitive feelings in people - sadism, guilt, masochism and so on - psychoanalysis has often made the hazardous inference that those infantile conflicts cause war, or that war is required as a kind of safety valve for them. The psychoanalyst might argue that any other causes of war that are adduced - such as social conflicts over material resources - are themselves either reducible to ‘repressed psychic contents’, or do not address the primitive feeling level in the adult, and therefore do not concern psychoanalysis. But that does not mean that those social forces are irrelevant to our overall understanding of war. The aims of psychoanalysis, psychotherapy and any psychological discipline are quite distinct from those of a ‘theory of war’. To put it simply, there may be non-psychological causes of war which such a theory has to take into account. To say that such causes are only rationalisations or externalisations of primitive psychic structures amounts to the claim that only the psyche exists. L'etat, c'est moi! This might lead to the Utopian and ill-founded view that war can be prevented by individuals being analysed.

Psychotherapists-In-Training Evaluate their Personal Therapy: Results of a UK Survey

Norman Macaskill and Ann Macaskill

Ann Macaskill

Ann Macaskill  

A national survey of the personal therapy experiences of UK Senior Registrars in Psychotherapy found that 87% reported their personal therapy had a moderate to very positive effect on both their work with patients and in their personal lives. Positive effects included increased self-awareness (76%), increased self-esteem (47%) and reduction in symptoms (43%). The most common primary goals for personal therapy were personal growth and the resolutions of personal problems.

No trainees reported purely negative outcomes for their therapy but 38% reported some negative effects from their therapy. The main negative effects were psychological distress (29%) and marital or family stress (13%).

These results are discussed in relation to previous research on personal therapy.

Laurence Spurling

Laurence Spurling

London

Laurence Spurling  

This is a book about heroes, psychoanalytic heroes, of whom, claims Rudnytsky, we are all in need after Freud. Here is a telling moment from the life of Rudnytsky's hero, told by his wife:

CW: I think there's one famous episode in his life, when he was nine, and he looked in the mirror and he said, ‘I'm too nice’. And really, from this point he started coming bottom of his class. Blotting everything, blotting his copybook, shoving things around, torturing flies, pulling their wings off. You know, just doing naughty things.

Interviewer: Did he like naughtiness? Was he in favor of naughtiness?

C W: He wanted to find this other dimension in himself. ‘I'm too good! I'm coming top all the time! Everybody likes me too much! I must find the nastiness in myself!’

This is an excerpt from an interview given by Clare Winnicott in 1983, published here for the first time and which alone makes this book worthwhile. For Rudnytsky Donald Winnicott is the figure who best embodies the virtues of the vocation of psychoanalysis, a man fundamentally decent, whose idea of decency involves knowing about the nastiness in himself. Rudnytsky admires Winnicott's independence and openness of mind, his lack of interest in establishing disciples or a school. He considers Winnicott's theoretical contributions to be of paramount importance in the rewriting of classical Freudian theory in terms of object relations, with its focus on the maternal, environmental and pre-oedipal facets of experience, which were either underplayed or missed out by Freud. And he pays tribute to Winnicott's direct and unpretentious clinical style, his capacity to understand his patients and to put them in touch with their creativity in everyday living. What for Rudnytsky marks Winnicott out from so many other psychoanalysts is his basic optimism, his belief in human nature. So, one can imagine, it is characteristic of Winnicott that, when he looks in the mirror, he sees not the outward show of an inner progression towards death (Freud), nor an innate envy waiting to be unmasked (Klein), nor even an alienated and alienating ego born of misrecognition (Lacan), but something simply good - to be sure with that element of reaction-formation against what is ‘naughty’, as Winnicott himself aged 9 strove to catch hold of, but still something reflected back of himself which he could then use to discover what was not so visible.

I wondered why Robin Skynner entitled his collection of papers on training and consultation for the helping professions as surviving institutes rather than institutions. Surely most of us today are occupied with questions about surviving, or perhaps more importantly attempting to live creatively, in some form of institution - whether it be a family, a work setting, or even enormous societal establishments which seem nearly impossible to influence, such as the NHS, the Church or the Government. Skynner has something to say about life in all these different types of institutions, and yet he chooses to focus particularly on institutes, which are organisations devoted to promoting scientific or educational objectives. One might be tempted to think of institutes as more benign in their outlook since their stated tasks are to disseminate knowledge. Why, then, is Skynner concerned with survival within these supposedly generative organisations?

Dear Editor

We thought readers of your Journal would be interested to know that, in January 1992, a number of psychoanalytically oriented organisations met informally to consider the developments taking place in the UKSCP. They were concerned that the diversity of standards and trainings and the size of the Analytical Section (over 30 organisations) posed insuperable problems to the establishment of appropriately rigorous standards for trainings at all levels.

As a result of this meeting a Working Party was set up to make proposals for a new organisation and on 8th March The British Confederation of Psychotherapists was formed. It has now been agreed that the character of this organisation is best represented by the following sub-title: Psycho-Analysts, Analytical Psychologists and Psycho-Analytical Psychotherapists.

The aim of this organisation is to form a register of psychotherapists who have trained in one or other of these three related forms of psychotherapy and have been approved by the Registration and Ethics Committees of the BCP. These Committees are in the process of formulating standards. We hope to be in a position to publish a register, invite new organisations to apply and present a full report of the BCP's aims and constitution early in 1993.

Joscelyn Richards, Acting Chair of Committee of Institutions

Editorial Introduction

R Hinshelwood

R Hinshelwood

R Hinshelwood  

During the nineteenth century there were not many treatments for people suffering mental disorders. And those that did emerge usually disappeared fairly promptly for one reason or another. In the first quarter of the century phrenology was the great white hope. In the second quarter moral treatment was developed and expanded throughout the mental hospitals of the Western world. In the latter half of the century psychiatric ideas were bankrupt and there was deep therapeutic pessimism. This was largely because of the relentless development of the scientific approach which did not apply easily to people and to madness. By the end of the century psychiatric treatment was simply admission to the mental hospital; the mental hospital was the treatment. Although Henry Maudsley campaigned in the latter decades of the century for ambulant treatments and out-patient clinics, the professional pessimism of psychiatrists did not allow their development until just before the second world war.

Instead the treatment of mental disturbances was promoted more by neurologists than by psychiatrists. In the 1870s some French medical men began experimenting with the suspect techniques of hypnosis. This had always been shunned by the medical profession as the province of quacks. However, Jean-Martin Charcot, the most eminent neurologist in France and on a par with Hughlings Jackson in England, lent his prestige to a serious medical interest in hypnosis. He thought of the hypnotic trance as an experimental model of the degenerative processes he thought underlay mental disorders. However others in France, and a little later in Britain and particularly in the United States, began to be impressed by the suggestive element in hypnosis and its use as a therapeutic method. This was conducted, at first, on an out-patient basis, by neurologists on those patients they tended to see most. Those patients presented with bizarre abnormalities of neurological function but no damage to the nervous system. They were hysterical - a condition known from time immemorial but a particular feature of the nineteenth century society. The use of suggestion, developed from hypnosis, became a highly sophisticated and reputable method of psychotherapy under Pierre Janet from the 1880s onwards - the French school. Morton Prince in the United States followed, and there exists to this day an active school of hypnosis. In Britain the grip of scientific pragmatism that had started here, and in the nineteenth century had showed its value in the immense technological development and its economic exploitation, consigned hypnotism to continuing suspicion. It had fallen into disuse by the end of the century, and Janet's suggestive methods were only patchily introduced subsequently.

On the Eve of a Revolution: Freud's Concepts of Consciousness and Unconsciousness in ‘Studies on Hysteria’ and the ‘Project for a Scientific Psychology’

David Smith

David Smith

David Smith  

There are many points in Freud's development which have been hailed as watersheds. Among these have been the formulation of the seduction theory in 1896, the beginning of Freud's self-analysis in 1897, the completion of The Interpretation of Dreams in 1899 and the formulation of the second topography in 1923. In the present paper I will argue that Freud effected a hitherto unrecognised but nonetheless momentous shift during the year 1895. I believe that the ‘turn’ of 1895 was more crucial for the development of psychoanalysis than any of the other nodal points listed above, for the creation of a psychoanalytic theory of the mind would not have been possible in its absence. Strange as it may sound, Freud's transition of 1895 was philosophical in nature: it was a shift from one view of the relation between brain and mind to another. More specifically, at some point during 1895 Freud moved from Cartesian dualism to a materialistic indentity theory of psyche/soma.

What is the relevance of this thesis to the Studies on Hysteria? As the Studies was written whilst Freud was in the midst of transition it is itself a transitional work. Studies on Hysteria stands with one foot in the pre-psychoanalytic past and the other in the psychoanalytic future. An understanding of Freud's philosophical dilemma both enriches our appreciation of the Studies and illuminates its limitations.

Paradoxically, psychoanalysis seems to be rediscovering the psychological impact of the father and sexual difference via perversion, itself constituted by disavowal of their significance. Or so Paris-based psychoanalyst Joyce McDougall and US psychotherapist Louise Kaplan claim.

Both thereby draw on Freud's account of perversion, at least fetishism, as originating in the boy's use of an object to stand in for the mother's missing penis which otherwise seems to signify threat of his masturbation being punished with castration by the father. McDougall and Kaplan, however, reinterpret her lack in post-Freudian terms - as signifying not threat but the place where the father's penis comes into its ‘true phallic function’. It thereby disabuses the child of the illusion of itself completing the mother's desire - an illusion fostered by prior failure to negotiate pre-Oedipal issues of maternal separation and loss, and by the mother herself in so far as she belittles the father.

McDougall describes in these terms her patient, Professor K's compulsively repeated scenario involving beating his girlfriend's bare bottom. Not only were her genitals thus concealed. He also eluded sexual difference by himself commandeering the roles of both father and mother (symbolised by whip and buttocks). McDougall describes lesbianism in similar terms - as involving identification with the father in order both to escape an orally devouring and anally controlling mother, and to realise her idealised counterpart in a female lover. All too often, says McDougall, this involves self-demeaning identification with a denigrated image of the father, as repository of oral and anal impulses otherwise evoked by the mother. Better far, she goes on, to have positive internalisation of mother and parental couple. How else does one achieve the erotic cathexis of one's body necessary to masturbation and its creation of the illusion of hermaphroditism in the transitional space between the ideal of narcissistic self-sufficiency and the reality of lack?

‘No’ In Hysteria

Salomon Resnik

Salomon Resnik

Salomon Resnik  

Freud on/in Hysteria

From October 1885 to February 1886, Freud worked at the Salpetriere in Paris under Charcot. Freud was very impressed by Charcot's Tuesday lectures where he presented amongst others his fascinating, seductive, hysterical patient called Blanche. Freud was fascinated by Charcot-Blanche and by the impact of the hypnotic approach which allowed the patient to express herself. In fact Blanche Wittmann, Charcot's ‘prima donna’, had a double personality. Pierre Janet, one of the attendants, was interested in the splitting of her personality and he used to think that Blanche Two was more balanced than Blanche One; a sort of inner rivalry?

Freud had already been impressed by Breuer's treatment of Fraulein Anna 0 between 1880 and 1882. The treatment of Anna 0 finished in June 1882, and in the following November Breuer related the remarkable story to Freud who was greatly impressed by it.

When Freud arrived back in Vienna from Paris in 1886, and settled down with his practice, a large proportion of his clientele were hysterics. At that time he used to recommend hydrotherapy, electrotherapy, massage and the Weir Mitchell rest-cure. Freud, impressed by Charcot and Dr Liebeault from Nancy in Bernheim's clinic, tried to use hypnosis on those patients. This method did not last long with Freud because he was aware that his personality was not sufficiently adapted to this method, in addition to other reasons that he discovered during the birth and early development of his psychoanalytic theory and practice.

Some years ago I was asked to write on hysteria for an important Italian encyclopedia (Enciciopedia Einaudi).

Hysterical phenomena were described in the Kahun papyrus (1900) as a woman's illness provoked by the spontaneous displacement of the uterus which behaves like a confused little animal wandering inside the body. The image of the ‘wandering uterus’ corresponds to a very archaic fantasy which Hippocrates takes up in the chapter of his book entitled ‘Women's illnesses’. It seems that the fantasy of getting rid of such a disturbing internal object ‘called uterus’ and an early cathartic therapeutic method was intuitively suggested by the author when he advises that: ‘when a woman who is afflicted with hysteria or who is in difficult labour, sneezes, it should be regarded as a good sign’.

Robert Tollemache  

We use the terms ‘narcissism’ and ‘narcissistic’ constantly but what do we really mean by them? The closer we look, the more elusive, also the more crucial, the idea seems to be. And how central is narcissism to Freud's thinking? What Freud meant and what we mean are so interrelated that we cannot think about one issue without also considering the other. This book provides considerable help in reaching conclusions about both issues. The International Psychoanalytic Association deserve thanks for commissioning this useful collection of essays based on ‘On Narcissism.’

The contributors come from all over Europe, the USA and Argentina, and represent both their local interests and the various psychoanalytic schools of thought. They were all asked to draw out the important points and link the paper with our present state of knowledge, so certain themes, such as the inadequacies of the libido theory and the developing concept of the ego, come up repeatedly. However each author has his or her own approach and perspective, therefore the repetition is not frustrating. It is, however, a challenging book; ‘On Narcissism’ is hard to read, for reasons which I will explain; and each author uses his or her space fully with a close critique of the paper. But do not be put off as the hard work is amply repaid.

‘On Narcissism’ is the first paper and reading the other papers makes it clear why it is a demanding read.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

London

Paul Gordon  

The British political left has never really had much time for psychoanalysis or psychotherapy, even though the personal beliefs and convictions of many analysts and therapists would place them at least somewhere on the left. Things have changed, of course, during the past 20 years or so as a great many feminists and socialists have turned to psychoanalysis both as theory, in attempts to explain more fully the mechanisms of oppression and to account for the apparent halt, however temporary, of the project of emancipation, and as therapy to come to terms with more personal matters. But the mainstream socialist project as such, it seems to me, has been largely untouched by the concerns and insights of psychoanalysis, and those leftists who profess an interest in. it tend to be seen if not as apostles, then as the disappointed, the men and women of too little faith.

Until the founding of the ‘Free Associations’ project in the early 1980s, one of the few places on the British left with any real interest in psychoanalysis was the journal New Left Review and its book publishing arm, New Left Books. It was one of the Review's editors Perry Anderson who, in a justly famous essay, ‘Components of the national culture’ (1969) bemoaned the fact that psychoanalysis had had such a vestigial impact on the general culture, being sealed off as a ‘technical enclave … an esoteric and specialised pursuit’. And it was the Review, not any psychoanalytic journal, which first published Lacan in English, and there too, at least for a time, that the ideas of David Cooper and R D Laing found a hearing. So too, did New Left Books publish Octave Mannoni's monograph on Freud as well as the work of Timpanaro.

Two of the key essays which make up Michael Rustin's book, published by Verso, the imprint of New Left books, were themselves first published in New Left Review (although the details in the book of which chapters were published before, and where, are incorrect) and the book itself represents a decade's work in linking, as the title says, the good society envisioned by socialism and the inner world as seen by psychoanalysis.

The Silence of Symbiosis: The Difficulty in Separating a Silent Adolescent Daughter and an Uncommunicative Mother

Paul Tibbles and Gillian Russell

Gillian Russell

Bloomburg Street, London SW1

Blackshaw Road, London SW 17

Gillian Russell  

This paper describes short-term psychotherapeutic intervention with an adolescent girl and her mother by two co-therapists. Intervention revealed an enmeshed, symbiotic relationship with the daughter's periods of mutism reflecting anger towards others, particularly her uncommunicative mother. The daughter's two-year history of hearing ‘voices’ had commenced as her mother's ‘voices’ had ceased, and seemed to represent a ‘magical’ attempt to fuse symbiotically with her. In therapy, as the mother started to talk about her own and her daughter's family background, the daughter became more verbally and emotionally communicative, and her ‘voices’ began to fade. As the daughter came to understand her mother more, and as the mother came to terms with her own past, they began to show some evidence of separating. Two issues were raised by the case: the importance of the initial contact between patient and insititution; and the difficulty in changing symbiotic relationships.
