Marie Bridge  

I was pleased to discover this collection because I had previously known of Joan Riviere only as the author of her famous 1935 paper, ‘A contribution to the analysis of the negative therapeutic reaction’. I was curious to know what else had been written by the author of such an important paper and to know something of the personality behind the thinking.

This volume consists of her collected papers 1920-1958. Its contents range from short book reviews to full-length psycho-analytic articles. Mrs Riviere's works are prefaced by a long scholarly introduction by Athol Hughes which places her life and works within the psychoanalytic, intellectual and social context of the time. We are given a rounded picture of her socially and professionally; we see her kindness and her astuteness, but also her snobbery and the lack of confidence that underlay this trait. We are also told something of the difficulties, especially about boundaries, in her analysis with Ernest Jones.

The book contains several major papers and it is interesting to follow the development of Riviere's own ideas. ‘Womanliness as a masquerade’ examines how a too perfect adjustment to traditional female roles can be a mask that hides anxiety about the woman's male identification and, especially, about the revenge she fears from both sexes because of her theft, in phantasy, of the penis which is an attack on mother as well as father. The theme of intense oral envy of the parents is developed in her 1932 paper, ‘Jealousy as a mechanism of defence’, where she shows, by close monitoring of the context of her patient's jealous outbursts, that ‘jealousy serves as a more ego-synotic substitute for envy’. Here she anticipates Mrs Klein's later work.

Kate Osborne

Kate Osborne

France

Kate Osborne  

This is a book on early attachment which examines both sides of the relationship, looking at what parents contribute in terms of their personal histories and expectations of parenthood, as well as what babies bring with them in terms of their responsiveness and adaptability. Hence there is a potentially fruitful collaboration between Berry Brazelton, renowned for his research on early infant development, and Bertrand Cramer, a psychoanalyst specialising in parent/infant relationships. Brazelton's work is already well documented and resumed here in the main part of the book. He describes his observations on the range of babies' reflexive behaviours, showing how complex and rapid are their adaptations to the environment in which they emerge. He is especially interested in the vast differences in reactivity and behavioural organisation between babies, which means that each baby has to be adjusted to in a different way by parents and professional carers, defying ready-made ‘formulae’ approaches to infant care. Despite the availability of this research, much medical discourse offered to parents during the early days of their relationship with their babies still seems to focus on ‘The Baby’ as a single individual, as if miraculously cloned at each birth. There is still little attention paid to discovering the individual differences in the feeding, sleeping and arousal patterns of young babies, and much damage is done to mothers' intuitive responses to their babies by standardised advice-giving.

Brazelton's work is therefore vastly important and made even more relevant when seen in the context of the parental part of the relationship. Bertrand Cramer contributes some well-chosen descriptions of the psychodynamic processes involved in both the desire for a child and accompanying a pregnancy. He writes briefly about the differences during pregnancy between mothers' and fathers' emotional attachment to the future child, and argues consistently for the increased participation of potential fathers in the obstetric process. Later in the book Cramer describes the symbolic place in the family dynamic played by each baby, pointing out some of the more common fantasies held by parents about their babies. He focuses particularly on those concerning the baby's disappearance or death, and of parental projections of the baby as sibling, parent or judge of the parents themselves. He also describes the commonly experienced reenactment of past relationships with each new child, especially as they are manifested in conflicts involving feeding, sleep patterns, and the rate of the child's development towards greater autonomy.

Training and Outcome in Supervised Individual Psychotherapy

Alasdair Macdonald

Alasdair Macdonald

Dumfries DG1 4TG

Alasdair Macdonald  

Fifty-three cases are reported. Thirty-five were offered psychotherapy but 10 left treatment early. Nine patients refused psychotherapy and nine were unsuitable. Outcome was measured by change in contacts with local health services and general practitioners for an equivalent time period before and after psychotherapy or assessment. Of the treatment group, 17 recovered, three were improved, one was unchanged and four were worse (P << 0.00 1). There was a reduction in general practice use by those who received even brief treatment. Those with anxiety symptoms improved most. The ‘refuser’ group contained more depressed patients and patients with alcohol or personality problems did less well. Variables not associated with outcome were: duration of treatment, previous treatment, therapist experience, therapist gender, number of cases previously seen and premature termination. Therapist prediction of outcome was not usually valid. Costs compared favourably with the costs of other forms of treatment.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Reflections on a Century of Freud: Some Paths Not Chosen

James Grotstein

James Grotstein

James Grotstein  

The title of this contribution could just as easily have been ‘Reflections on the Freudian Century’ so extensive and profound have been the influence of this one man and his ideas. That psychoanalysis has persevered long enough to celebrate its centennial constitutes a rare achievement in itself. Psychoanalysis, despite the continuing attacks against it, has become an integral part of universal culture. It not only enjoys an established position in the fields of medicine, behavioural sciences and critical studies, albeit not without controversy; it has penetrated into the interstices of our daily lives in countless ways, whether we consider the rise in the valorisation our culture affords individual emotional life, the advocacy of children, the rise in female consciousness, the change in family values, the sexual revolution, etc. In fact, there was a time not so long ago when virtually every department head of psychiatry in American universities had been trained as an analyst. There has occurred a vast recessional from that golden age in our country. The rise in importance of neurobiology and psychopharmacology was one notable reason. Another was the natural attrition of an idea which had not renewed itself in the temper of the times. Much of what I wish to say has to do with the theme of psychoanalytic attrition and renewal, that is, a reassessment of the essence of Freud's contributions with the idea of conducting samples of respectful deconstructions that might lead to new avenues of exploration.

One of the problems of any new field is the inherent tendency of stagnation and entropy to invade it. I believe that this is one of the principal meanings Freud had in mind when he conceived of his unfortunately ill-received death instinct (Freud 1920). (Yet Freud may probably have been on to something which his followers failed to understand and which Klein may have overenthusiastically misunderstood - that the quintessence of Freud's concept of the death instinct refers to decay, which is what psychoanalysis is in danger of suffering from.) The quest for legitimacy in the troubled time of its origins led Freud to apostolise his followers and hold them to a sacred covenant, thereby reducing the dialectical atmosphere of debate and contention that was necessary for the healthy growth and expansion of any new idea. (Here I have in mind Freud's part in the unfortunate ‘defections’ of Jung, Adler and Rank as well as his depreciation of the work of Melanie Klein - or, for that matter, his rejection of those inside the movement who disagreed with him.) His ‘loyal’ followers then standardised, legitimatised and defended his works, let alone constrained them into analytic institute catechisms, resulting in their sanitation and gentrification.

Psychoanalysis and War

Isobel Hunter-Brown

Isobel Hunter-Brown

Isobel Hunter-Brown  

Ms Birkett is to be congratulated on bringing to our attention important issues regarding Psychoanalysis and War (British Journal of Psychotherapy 8(3)). My own feeling like hers is that it would be good to see more psychoanalytic contributions on the effects of militarism (and of the lessening of humanitarianism in our present day society too). There are, however, a number of aspects of her article which require response.

She begins with two criticisms of psychoanalysis (1) that, generally, it should have had more to say on the effects of social changes on the individual psyche and (2) that it has an addiction to infantile fantasy and ignores the impact of current realities. In particular she mentions the realities of persecution, war, migration and the concentration camp and holocaust.

She conveys the impression that psychoanalysts have only recently begun to realise the damage wrought by these disasters but, though there may be a relative paucity of literature, psychoanalysts have been writing about them for many years. Contributions are too numerous to mention but in 1968 a series of papers for a conference on the effects of social disaster was included in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis. On the nuclear threat, a six-page bibliography was published in the International Review of Psychoanalysis (1987) which included psychoanalytic papers dating back to 1946.

It is perhaps true as Ms Birkett says that Bettelheim is the only psycho-analyst to have written from his personal concentration camp experience, though in many ways others suffered greatly. It was a by-word after the barbarities of the First World War that ex-servicemen typically maintained a life-long silence on their sufferings. The effect of enduring horrors not shared by others seems to cause this reaction. Anna Freud dealt with her experience of becoming a ‘displaced person’ by offering help to certain of the most vulnerable and impressionable of her host country's displaced persons - babies - for whom she set up several residential nurseries in London. Her writings show how she gave weight to the impact on the infants of war-time external realities, including the reality of their mothers' attitudes, as affecting their developing psychological functioning. All psychoanalysts, however, do stress that ‘the eye brings with it what it sees’, Kleinians particularly emphasising the phantasy element. It must not be forgotten too that phantasies forged in experience precipitate some of the events of external reality. What happens when a person perceives that an external reality threatens to approximate to a wish-fulfilling fantasy derived from a dangerous (e.g. murderous) wish is that the fantasy may be repressed or other defensive measures may be instituted.

The Baby Makers: An In-Depth Single-Case Study of Conscious and Unconscious Psychological Reactions to Infertility and ‘Baby-Making’ Technology

Joan Raphael-Leff

Joan Raphael-Leff

London NW3 2TD

Joan Raphael-Leff  

Recent innovations of interventive technologies of fertilisation (AIH, AID, IVF) have brought in their wake a wave of psychological reactions in the consumers. This new syndrome includes psychological symptoms such as derealisation, depersonalisation, hypochondria, low self-esteem, guilt and neurotic depression; anxiety reactions; phobic avoidance and obsessional reactions with rumination and compulsive rituals. In addition, considerable interpersonal stress is manifested within the marital/ intimate relationships of these patients who strive to ‘make’ a baby, rather than being able to just naturally ‘have’ one.

This presentation focuses on unconscious phantasies and dynamic processes underlying such symptomatology, including the emotional effects of being unable to treat intercourse as a twoperson generative event or the body as a creative fertile exponent of the self. Data is drawn from an in-depth study of 19 patients seen in 1-5 per week psychoanalysis or individual/couple therapy and a single case is presented in depth. Attention is focused on subfertile patients’ special transference relationship to the medical specialist - as ‘Baby Maker’.

[[RunningHead]]

Children under the Nazi Yoke

Judith Kestenberg

Judith Kestenberg

30 Soundview Lane, Sands Point, NY 11050

Judith Kestenberg  

This paper deals with the effect of persecution on children during the Holocaust. The psychic consequences discussed pertain to the Nazis' assault on the children's bodies, on their ego, their superego and their identity. A brief section summarises problems of psychotherapy for child survivors and the last part deals with the consequences of Nazi ideology on the superego of Germans.

Starvation and other forms of interference with the functioning of the body deplete narcissism and destroy the will to live. Ways of rekindling of narcissism and enhancing the will to live are discussed.

The effect of persecution on the ego is manifold. The restriction of space with the ensuing inability to move freely, the breaking down of the children's sense of gravity with the ensuing inability to stand up or stretch, the loss of the sense of time, all represented an infringement on basic ego functions, acquired during early development. Outstanding among their defences were numbing of affect, splitting and identification with the aggressor or frustrator. However, child survivors developed an amazing ability to adapt to new and stressful circumstances.

The effect of the lawlessness on the superego was especially difficult for young children and adolescents. Previously acquired rules had to be abandoned and a new set of rules had to be learned, rules which sanctified stealing as means of survival. Happily, after the return of adult guidance with their own ethical values restored, children and especially adolescents rebuilt their shattered and altered superego.

The most outstanding effect of persecution was the loss of one's identity, the loss of feeling of being worthwhile and an imposition of a new religion on hidden children, who had to disavow their Jewishness to survive.

The persecution of non-Jewish children differed from the assault on the Jewish children's identity. Jews were destined to die while others were either enslaved, made to conform or even chosen to be Germanized. Many Jewish children in hiding were raised in the spirit of Christian teachings which blamed the Jews for killing the Saviour. Treatment should aim at helping the Jewish child-survivors to regain confidence in their own memories and to raise their shattered self-esteem.

Lastly a short section deals with the way Nazis brought up their own children and distorted their superego. Grandiosity and taking advantage of the Jews to project their own guilt on them fostered lawlessness. It is suggested that the Nazis hated their own children whom they sent to war and killed when they were handicapped. This hatred was repressed and projected upon Jews. The Jews may have been chosen as scapegoats because they developed ethics which prohibited child sacrifice and thus rescued children from death, a tenet incompatible with an ideology that advocates child killing.

The Use of Audio and Videotape Recordings of Therapy Sessions in the Supervision and Practice of Dynamic Psychotherapy

Mark Aveline MD FRC

Mark Aveline

114 Thorneywood Mount, Nottingham NG3 2PZ

Mark Aveline  

The use of audio and videotape recordings in supervision of dynamic psychotherapy is controversial. Recordings give direct, factually correct access to the therapy session which cannot be matched by the common, indirect method in supervision of recollection. The arguments for and against taping are presented and the conclusion is reached that tapes are an essential aid in supervision. They facilitate the close examination of process and technique. Discrepancies between the recollected account and the record are highlighted, not with the purpose of showing up the deficiencies of the therapist but as phenomena that have meaning and significance. How the therapist deals with transference and emotionally-charged issues can be seen and discussed. Perhaps their greatest value is in private review by the therapist. The meaning of being taped needs to be carefully considered and monitored by the therapist. Taping should be used selectively and sensitively. Careful attention needs to be given to consent, confidentiality and the security of the tapes. Advice is given on how to make recordings. Tapes may also be used in teaching, research and clinical audit.

Psychoanalysis and War

Diana Birkett

Diana Birkett

95 Elspeth Road, London SW 11

Diana Birkett  

The earliest and some of the most creative developments in psychoanalysis took place in Europe at a time when the continent was devastated by two of the most destructive wars in history. Further, many of the most gifted practitioners and theorists in this field were, by virtue of their race or nationality, more than averagely affected by the splitting of families and the deaths of members resulting from fighting, persecution, invasion and separation.

One would think that any science which sought to explain human behaviour would be drawn to these issues. Yet they are addressed, in the psychoanalytic literature, almost exclusively in terms of the inner life of the individual. Psychoanalysis has curiously little to say about world events; in another context, that of political persecution in Argentina, Janine Puget (1988) comments: ‘the theoretical instrument does not allow for the formulation of theories about external reality’, though she does qualify this in relation to group analysis. Indeed, it was in the field of groups that Freud took a lead in applying the insights of psychoanalysis to an understanding of society. This represented a one-way process, however, and there was little attempt to study the effects of society on the psyche.

Perhaps this should come as no surprise. Psychoanalysis in its early days never claimed to be a political or social theory, and has always concentrated on the inner world of the individual as determined by infantile conflicts. From its inception it has striven to fend off the claims of real-life events (as in Freud's abandonment of the seduction theory). In a passage from ‘A Child is being Beaten’ (1919), Freud seems to be paying lip-service to the impact of events in later life:

at the present time theoretical knowledge is still far more important than therapeutic success, and anyone who neglects childhood analysis is bound to fall into the most disastrous errors. The emphasis which is laid here on the importance of the earliest experience does not imply any underestimation of the importance of later ones. But the later impressions of life speak loudly enough through the mouth of the patient, while it is the physician who has to raise hisvoice on behalf of the claims of childhood.

Communicative psychotherapy or psychoanalysis (Smith uses the terms interchangeably) is an attempt to restore the patient's voice which, argues Smith, all too often gets swallowed up in the discourse of the therapist. It claims to see things from the patient's point of view. This is not a new endeavour within psychoanalysis as is seen, for example, in a quotation from Margaret Little, which Smith justifiably describes as ‘one of the most memorable passages in the psychoanalytic literature on technique’ (p. 92):

We often hear of the mirror which the analyst holds up to the patient, but the patient holds one up to the analyst too, and there is a whole series of reflections in each, repetitive in kind and subject to continual modification.

Communicative psychotherapy, a type of therapy developed by Robert Langs, takes as its primary aim and purpose the uncovering, investigation and clarification, to both patient and therapist, of this mirror held up by the patient and within which the therapist can see a reflection of him/herself and his/her conduct of the therapy.

This mirror needs uncovering because it is nearly always kept under wraps. It shows itself indirectly and allusively, not in the explicit and conscious commentary which the patient makes on the therapist, but in other forms, notably in communications about other people. In the stories the patient tells about his or her life and the people in it, particularly those which have qualities of spontaneity and immediacy, the communicative therapist discovers hidden and unconscious communications about the patient's experience of the therapy. The patient's conversation is heard as a form of ongoing feedback to the therapist on the quality of his or her therapeutic skills and, indeed, his or her very suitability to be a therapist in the first place.

Lesley Caldwell  

This book gives a comprehensive overview of the theoretical developments in one strand of British psychoanalytic thinking and the individual contributions of its leading figures. This double focus is both its strength and its major frustration. Rayner, through a process of informed selection and construction, provides a valuable account of many thinkers while outlining and making an argument for the shared set of positions which unite in diversity a now established tradition. Historically and theoretically the author displays an impressive grasp of the area and, personally, he reveals a commitment to it which is inspiring. The Independent Mind is a clear guide to the debates and to the analysts who have shaped British psychoanalysis. Its chosen form seems to propose it as a compendium, an enumeration of positions, but it is rather more than that. In its delineation of a set of common concerns it elaborates and defines a discursive arena along with the practices that have supported it and the issues which have made it distinctive. Rayner, in selecting and discussing Independent concerns, further establishes that group and its emphases: he gives us a coherence marked by a loosely shared set of concerns. In doing so he becomes one of the architects of its chosen domain, both past and future.

Of equal interest is the perspective Rayner offers on the distinctiveness of the British school. He insists on the peculiarly British heritage of the analysts he discusses, arguing for their place in a tradition of experimentation, of testing, and of the authenticity of experience. His approach here is somewhat at odds with the orientation of much recent philosophical and social theorising, but it sets an agenda for further socio-cultural discussions of the place of psychoanalysis in British cultural and theoretical debate and of the emergence of its specific concerns. For, in describing one group, Rayner also succeeds in demonstrating the common positions which inform a national orientation.

Hysteria - A Contemporary Kleinian Perspective

David Bell

David Bell

David Bell  

It is commonly held that hysteria, in terms of full conversion syndromes, is much less frequently observed today at least in the ‘developed’ world and, although many have seriously questioned the value of the continued use of the diagnosis, it seems that the term, as Lewis (1975) remarked, will long outlive its obituarists.

Patients who come for analysis today tend to have less flamboyant symptomatology. They are preoccupied with feelings of emptiness and alienation and we understand them as suffering from narcissistic disorders or borderline conditions. I will contend, however, in this paper, that the basic psychopathology and central preoccupations of these patients are not essentially different from those patients studied by Freud and Breuer. It is the manifestations of this psychopathology which have altered although, in the privacy of the analytic consulting room, transient conversion syndromes, hysterical identifications, indeed the full gamut of ‘hysterical’ symptoms are, I think, less uncommon than is sometimes held.

In the famous ‘Preliminary Communication’, Breuer and Freud (1893) draw conclusions from their consideration of hysterical phenomena which formed the foundations of the theory and technique of psycho-analysis: the concept of repression makes its first appearance and elsewhere in ‘Studies on Hysteria’ the terms ‘unconscious’ and ‘transference’ are used for the first time in a psycho-analytic sense. For the purposes of the present paper, I wish firstly to draw attention to an essential component of Freud and Breuer's conceptualisation of hysteria which in contemporary psycho-analytic thinking has been extraordinarily fruitful.

They state:

… we have become convinced that the splitting of consciousness which is so striking in the well-known classical cases under the form of ‘double consciousness’ is present to a rudimentary degree in every hysteria and that a tendency to such a dissociation, and with it the emergence of abnormal states of consciousness (which we shall bring together under the term ‘hypnoid’), is the basic phenomenon of this neurosis.

I Was a Shoah Child

Yolanda Gampel

Yolanda Gampel

Pilichovski 32, Ramat Aviv, 69431 Israel

Yolanda Gampel  

This paper deals with the struggle to live despite massive traumatic events among individuals who were children during World War Two. The material for the paper was taken from a series of interviews with Shoah child survivors who were drawn from a non-clinical population. The interviews attempted to explore how the Shoah experience affected some of the natural expressions of feeling that are universal in childhood. More specifically, the paper focuses on crying, dreams and treasured objects. The picture which emerged from the interviews is consistent. In the face of the terrifying and traumatic reality of the Shoah, the ego of the Shoah child was forced to function automatically and without expression of feeling. Through the creation of a ‘false self’ these children were able to function as adults, in the bodies of children, thereby enabling their survival. Inordinate capacities to struggle and to manage without the comfort of tears and teddy bears were evidenced by these child-adults.

A Brief Personal Memoir of Wilfred Bion

John Hill

John Hill

9 Crediton Hill, London NW3 1HT

John Hill  

I first met Bion in 1949, knew him socially for some years and then, in the course of analytic training, went to him for supervision of my second case some nine years later and continued this for several years after qualification. In the course of supervision, as in some of his writing, he tended to emphasise the importance of not making undue efforts to remember specific ideas, but would say instead: ‘Let the patient remind you’. I have found this comment pertinent to his own ideas and, in over thirty years of analysing, supervising and teaching, I have found myself both with patients and perhaps particularly with students reminded more often of things that Bion has said than any other single source of my inspiration. It is because I have found myself in this way so often reminded of Bion that I have been moved to write this short paper, not with any idea of a systematic evaluation but rather anecdotally to describe some of his perceptions that have come most frequently to my own mind in the course of both treating patients and teaching students.

My experience was that Bion's technique as a supervisor differed sharply from others; in particular from those supervisors who combined an insistence that their students should not take notes during sessions with a requirement that in supervision they should attempt rigorously to reproduce the minute by minute, word by word detail of the session. Whether this is still widely practised I do not know but even then it seemed to me that such a requirement was perhaps impossible to the point of absurdity. In contrast Bion would sometimes say: ‘Don't take notes, keep a diary and on those days when you curse the day you ever heard of psychoanalysis put that down in your diary’. He reminds me of a lecturer in philosophy at Oxford (Gilbert Ryle) who would tell his students that if he caught anyone taking notes in his lectures he would send them out for inattention.

I was never quite able to put his advice about the diary into practice but here I must put my association with Bion into a broader personal context. I came across him originally through belonging to the Tavistock Institute of Human Relations where the lady who was to become his wife worked with me on a data team attached to the Glacier project. In that atmosphere, at that time, what was startling, disturbing and ultimately refreshing, particularly coming from one of his analytic eminence, was that so far from idealising analysis he would calmly and openly express negative views about it with an awareness that by virtue of its being able to do good it was also able to be harmful and, while he would acknowledge that envy might sometimes play a part in this process, ‘I don't personally put the word in neon lights on my consulting room ceiling’.

London

Francesca Raphael  

The Handbook of Art Therapy is the most recent of a number of books aimed at opening up the theory and practice of art therapy to a wider audience. It is an ambitious book in that it covers a huge territory of discussion, ranging from detailed practical considerations, such as room lay-out, to the more in-depth exploration of theory and ideas. This combination gives a somewhat uneven texture to the book. The reader is expected to be both a novice who might benefit from simple, practical information, and yet also a sophisticated practitioner, familiar with the central tenets of psychoanalytic thinking. Notwithstanding this unusual mix, the book succeeds in giving a flavour of art therapy as practised in Britain today. Indeed, perhaps this mix is a reflection of that practice, addressing both practical and theoretical issues as they arise in clinical work.

A consistent theme throughout the book is the authors' assertion that art therapy practice derives from and is governed by psychoanalytic principles. A significant proportion of the book is devoted to tracing the influence of psychoanalytic thinking on the art therapist's understanding of aesthetics, symbolism and art. Despite the depth and breadth of these discussions, some of the clinical examples suggest that psychoanalytical principles and techniques are not yet fully integrated into art therapy practice. An example may illustrate the point.

A five-year-old boy came to his session and was dismayed to find a small hole in the clay cup that he had made previously. On discovering the damage he cried out: ‘Oh no! It's broken!’ to which the art therapist replied: ‘Don't worry, it doesn't look broken to me. We can mend it’.

A more analytically informed response might have explored and acknowledged the child's evident anxiety and distress in the face of a damaged container, both literally (the clay cup) and in the transference.

In contrast to this, the discussion of art therapy with groups shows far greater sensitivity and insight into the practical application of psychoanalytic concepts. Drawing on the work of Foulkes, Bion and Main, the authors show clearly how art therapy groups have grown out of analytic thinking. The clinical vignettes bring the theory to life and demonstrate an effective integration of theory and practice.

It is entirely admirable that we should aim to become better psychotherapists. But where this becomes an obsession with the correctness of therapeutic technique it may prove counter-productive. Too great a striving for perfection on the part of the psychotherapist does not help the patient; it only re-enacts the compulsion to perfection from which the patient himself very likely suffers. Not only is it human to err: error itself, and the capacity to recover from it, can provide both therapist and patient with unique opportunities for insight and personal growth.

Two or Three Sessions? A Discussion of Some Ideas about the Frequency of Sessions in Psychotherapy

Ruth Barnett

Ruth Barnett

73 Fortune Green Road, London NW6 1DR

Ruth Barnett  

In this paper I explore some issues involved in attempting to assess whether there are definable differences, beneficial or otherwise, between psychotherapy at two times and three times a week. I question the common assumption that more is better and I explore whether there is good reason to formulate such an hypothesis and how far it might be tested and evaluated. Firstly, I consider the number of sessions we have ourselves experienced in our training therapies. Secondly, I look at some assumptions we make about the work we do with our patients with regard to number of sessions per week and I illustrate this with material from some of my own patients. Thirdly, I attempt to draw this discussion together around the question of the optimum number of sessions per week. I conclude that there are some discernable differences between the work in two or three sessions a week. Assessment of their benefits and/or disadvantages is more difficult and open to the influence of ideological assumptions and prejudices. My material shows that the frequency of sessions may have rather different meanings for different patients. Nor will therapists necessarily agree on how the different use made of two or three sessions is to be regarded.

Maxine Anderson  

Daniel Stern's book The Interpersonal World of the Infant is reviewed with some detail paid to his notion of the sequential unfolding of the subjective experience of self during infancy. He denotes this sequence as the Senses of the Self and they include the Sense of an Emergent Self (birth-2 months of age); Sense of Core Self (2-6 months); Sense of Subjective Self (7-15 months); Sense of a Verbal Self (15 months on). A critical evaluation of Stem's conclusions is offered - several issues which the author feels are valuable contributions to our growing understanding of infancy, and several which illuminate, in the author's opinion, the unavoidable element in research that the researcher is influenced by his own ‘basic truths’, in this instance the legacy of the American ego-psychologic tradition.

This paper will review the work of Daniel Stern as encompassed within his book The Interpersonal World of the Infant, beginning with an overview of what I feel this work conveys and contributes. Then I will offer some thoughts about possibly significant underpinnings of his point of view about human development.

Clinical Commentary XIII

The therapist writes:

[This section is a regular feature. A short piece of clinical material from an actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the case. The material has been sent ‘blind’ to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention is to put these commentaries on the same material side by side for comparison of the different approaches and to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice - Ed]

The Patient

The patient is a man of 40, a member of a religious community for around 10 years, and has been a practising homosexual since childhood. Following a period of exhibitionism and sexual contact in public toilets, he was seen by a colleague and then referred on as he wished to ‘unpack’ a number of issues. He expressed uncertainty with the (un)structure of therapy, but after five sessions indicated some relief, a little emotional release and a desire to continue with the work. Therapy commenced on a once-weekly basis, later increasing to twice- and then thrice-weekly at the patient's request, and has continued for some 2′/2 years.

History/Background

J's family background is complex, and because of a problem of ‘betraying loyalty’ it has emerged only gradually. He describes himself as illegitimate - a ‘love child’ - and was raised by his mother, a fiery, possessive and powerful woman, his grandma and one or two aunts. His father, already married, was a remote, older man who visited periodically, and the family relationships were stormy, with his parents unable to have a consistent union. His father died when he was eight and his recollection of him is vague. He was prevented from attending the funeral and remembers his mother's wild grief occupying the emotional space afterwards. He has referred to his own existence as ‘a skeleton in her/ the cupboard’, of ‘not being wanted’ and of a sense of his mother's preference for a girl (and then it would have been ‘all right’).

Clinical Lectures on Klein and Bion edited by Robin Anderson. Published by Routledge, London, 1991; 139 pages; £9.99.

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

London

Bob Hinshelwood  

These nine lectures were all given by senior Kleinian psycho-analysts on three study days organised by the Institute of Psycho-Analysis in London. Six lectures were on Klein, and three on Bion. An introduction of an historical kind has been added by Robin Anderson, the editor of this published collection. The lectures were conceived as a whole for a ‘mixed audience’ to present the ideas and the practice of current Kleinian psycho-analysts. Each lecture gives a practical feel to the ideas by illustrating every step with clinical material.

This is a major work in that the most senior practitioners have been asked to cover systematically the scope of Kleinian discoveries and to present them in a form that is accessible to the interested public. I approached the book with the intention of liking it and applauding it; and I finished it with the belief that my preconceived judgement had been confirmed. I was satisfied. I had a good read.

There is no doubt that the book succeeds in giving an important insight into the way Kleinians think, and the way these thoughts are put into action in the consulting room. The lectures do not compromise on the complexities; they do not ‘talk down to their audiences' as Hanna Segal's foreword points out (p. ix). The twin objectives of engaging with complexity and accessibility to the public creates a tension for the reader (and authors) which is highly fruitful at the best moments. These are where the author takes us into the deeply intricate twists and turns of the details of the material of their patient. Notable in this regard are the chapters by Irma Brenman-Pick on early objectrelations in the psycho-analytic setting, the two on projective identification by Elizabeth Bott Spillius and Michael Feldman, and Edna O’ Shaughnessy's guided tour into the world of psychosis.

At other times the tension degenerates for a moment to the easy use of technical jargon - ‘from the beginning of life the infant, in phantasy, introjects his mother's breast and repeatedly splits its good and bad aspects with the aim of introjecting the good ones and projecting and annihilating the bad ones’ (p. 19). Many, or most, of the words used in this sentence have special technical meaning and allusions -‘beginning of life’, ‘phantasy’, ‘introjection’, ‘breast’, ‘splitting’, ‘good aspects’, ‘bad aspects’, ‘projection’ and ‘annihilation’. Such a sentence has little real explanatory value for those who need to learn these special meanings and for those who already know them. To quote such a sentence from this book may be a little unfair since, on the whole, it is just this kind of jargon which the book is trying to fill out with life and meaning. The clinical material is presented vividly in order to give a flesh and blood existence to such jargon.

These two volumes - the first a series of sensitive yet rigorously probing interviews between Didier Anzieu and Gilbert Tarab, and the second, papers on a range of psychoanalytic, cultural and aesthetic themes - form ‘envelopes’ for the exploration of the closely-bonded conceits, ‘psychic envelope’ and ‘skin ego’. The Empty Core: An Object Relations Approach to Psychotherapy of the Schizoid Personality by Jeffery Seinfeld. Published by Jason Aronson Inc., New Jersey, 1991; 260 pages; £28.50.

David Mann

David Mann

London

David Mann  

Jeffery Seinfeld is an American psychotherapist working within the British Object Relations tradition, particularly with the concepts of Fairbairn and Winnicott. Seinfeld acknowledges his debt to Fairbairn, stating the fact tht since his papers in the 1940s nobody has mapped the schizoid mind as clearly as Fairbairn. Unlike Harry Guntrip, however, Seinfeld is prepared to have a critical appreciation of Fairbairn's theories. For example, he takes issue with Fairbairn who always maintained he could not see why a satisfied infant would need to internalise the object. Seinfeld suggests this view overlooks the adaptive, creative aspects of internalisation and the development of psychic structure. This is reflected in his clinical discussions and recommendations: the fundamental schizoid splits serve adaptive as well as defensive purposes.

The book, as the title suggests, is primarily an attempt to describe the clinical experience of working with schizoid states and the particular difficulties this entails in the psychotherapy setting. Seinfeld notes, as Fairbairn did before him, that schizoid states account for the majority of clients seen in psychotherapy. As he writes in the Preface (p. x): ‘The purpose of this volume is to show how to overcome one of the greatest obstacles to psychotherapy - the schizoid dread of potentially good object relations’.

Seinfeld's principal thesis is that at the heart of the schizoid mind is an empty core. The schizoid individual complains of feeling isolated, disengaged, unconnected and apathetic. S/he has a consuming desire for object dependence but attachment threatens the loss of self. Such individuals protect themselves by emotional withdrawal. Summarising Fairbairn, Seinfeld describes the infant's process when s/he feels unloved and that her/his love is not valued. The infant comes to view her/his love as bad and love directed outward as destructive. To keep her/his love good s/he directs it inwards. The child concludes that love relationships are not to be trusted. Seinfeld then suggests that love is felt as emptiness; physiological hunger becomes a metaphor for the psychic state associated with a lack of love. The empty core is (p. 8): ‘the sense of lack or fissure in a primitive, sensory dominated, presymbolic state of boundedness more primitive than the internal world’. This empty core is endless, a shapeless space due to lack of boundedness, and it threatens the dissolution of being. Seinfeld makes links with other theoretical positions which describe an inner void such as existential phenomenology, Sartre's description of nothingness as a hole in the plenitude of being, and post-modernist philosophy which speaks of the void that remains between signifier and signified. The empty core, initially experienced as the lack of instinctual need, becomes the uncrossable divide between the external and the internal object world. Seinfeld stresses that this is not entirely a negative experience: the experience of emptiness also generates ego interests, ambitions and ideals. Here Seinfeld introduces Winnicott's idea of a permanently non-communicating, unknown private self at the core. He cites Sophocles' Oedipus of Colonus, when Oedipus says to his daughter: ‘When I am nothing/So then I am a man?’. The void provides freedom to shape ourselves. However, if the disruption becomes too traumatic or prolonged for the infant the empty core may become the bottomless pit of the schizoid client. Seinfeld does not seem to make clear why the infant should have a void or emptiness at the core of the personality.

Sublimation: Inquiries into Theoretical Psychoanalysis by Hans W Loewald. Published by Yale University Press, 1988; 89 pages; £12.50.

David Mann

David Mann

London

David Mann  

This short, interesting book by one of America's leading ego psychologists attempts to get to grips with one of the most elusive of psychoanalytical concepts, sublimation. Loewald makes the point early on that sublimation has both a privileged and a suspect status in psychoanalysis. The privileged status is due to human self-evaluation. It is suspect insofar as psychoanalysis tends to regard modes of psychic life as a defence, a concealment of true psychic reality.

Loewald traces the development of the concept of sublimation through Freud's thinking when it was first mentioned by him in the 1890s in the Fliess letters. There Freud speaks of phantasies as ‘psychical facades constructed in order to bar the way to these memories’, but he also asserts that ‘phantasies at the same time serve the trend towards refining memories, towards sublimating them’ (p. 1). Loewald shows convincingly that this enigmatic status of sublimation remained to the end of Freud's life.

Loewald goes on to trace the development of thought about sublimation. Traditionally it has been classified as a defence, but not pathological. Fenichel distinguished successful defences under the term sublimation and unsuccessful defences as pathogenic. Sublimation in this respect is successful in that, under the influence of the ego, the aim or object is changed without blocking adequate discharge. Complications arise in trying to decide whether sublimation is a higher or lower form of psychic organisation. The former includes valued cultural functions such as religious, moral and artistic achievement, the latter being all forms of psychic functioning that go beyond the immediate pursuit of direct instinctual discharge without being affected, thereby becoming unsuccessful defences.
